# Silicon: How an Oxide Built the Modern World

## Introduction

Silicon is not the best semiconductor. Germanium conducted better in the earliest transistors, and gallium arsenide is faster in many applications. Silicon won because of something less obvious: its oxide. Silicon dioxide grows cleanly on the surface of the crystal, insulates well, and can be patterned with great precision. That property made cheap, scalable manufacturing possible, and manufacturability, not electronic performance, put silicon at the center of modern technology.

Silicon is the second most abundant element in Earth's crust, about 28 percent by mass, yet for most of history it was valued only as sand, clay, and stone. Today it is the substrate of the processors that dominate computing and of most of the world's solar panels. This essay follows silicon from its chemistry and early uses through the semiconductor revolution and solar energy, and then tests the thesis against the challenges that now surround the element: environmental cost, a fragile supply chain, and the physical limits of miniaturization.

## Chemistry: Why the Oxide Matters

Silicon has atomic number 14 and sits directly beneath carbon in group 14. Like carbon, it has four valence electrons and forms four covalent bonds. It is a metalloid: its conductivity lies between that of metals and insulators, which is what makes it useful in electronics.

Silicon's defining chemical trait is its affinity for oxygen. The silicon-oxygen bond is very strong, so silicon never occurs free in nature. It is found as silica (quartz and sand) and in the silicate minerals, such as feldspars, micas, and clays, that make up most of the crust. The same strength has a cost: extracting the element requires reducing quartz with carbon in electric arc furnaces at temperatures above 1,900 °C, which yields metallurgical-grade silicon of about 98 to 99 percent purity. Silicon is abundant, but it is expensive in energy terms to free from oxygen.

The same affinity explains why silicon is not the basis of life, despite its resemblance to carbon. Silicon-silicon bonds are weaker than carbon-carbon bonds, and silicon's oxide is a rigid solid rather than a soluble gas like carbon dioxide. Silicon does form rich families of compounds, including silanes and silicones, but chains of silicon atoms are readily attacked by water and oxygen, and so cannot sustain the flexible chemistry of living cells. Life on Earth is carbon-based. Electronics, by contrast, turned silicon's attachment to oxygen into an asset.

## Early Uses: Glass, Ceramics, and the Slow Discovery of the Element

Humans used silicon compounds long before they understood the element. Flint and obsidian supplied the sharpest tools of the Stone Age. Mesopotamian and Egyptian artisans were making glass by melting sand with alkali fluxes thousands of years ago. Bricks, pottery, and porcelain are silicate ceramics, and Roman concrete and its modern descendant, Portland cement, depend on calcium silicates for their strength.

The element itself was identified much later. Antoine Lavoisier suspected in 1787 that silica was the oxide of an unknown element. Humphry Davy, and then Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Jacques Thénard, attempted to isolate it in the early 1800s, and Jöns Jacob Berzelius succeeded in obtaining amorphous silicon in 1823. He named it after the Latin *silex*, flint. For another century the element remained a laboratory curiosity and a metallurgical additive, used in steel and aluminum alloys. Its decisive role awaited an understanding of semiconductors.

## The Semiconductor Revolution

A semiconductor's conductivity can be controlled precisely by adding tiny amounts of impurities, a process called doping. Phosphorus supplies extra electrons and creates n-type material; boron creates electron deficiencies, called holes, and gives p-type material. Joining the two forms a p-n junction, the basis of diodes and transistors.

The first transistor was built at Bell Labs in 1947 by John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, with William Shockley developing the theory and the junction transistor that followed. It used germanium. Silicon devices appeared in the 1950s and soon overtook it. Silicon is more abundant and cheaper, and it tolerates higher temperatures. Above all, it forms a stable, insulating native oxide that can be grown directly on its surface. Germanium's oxide is water-soluble and poorly behaved, which made it unsuitable for the same treatment.

That difference decided the outcome. In 1959 Jean Hoerni at Fairchild Semiconductor developed the planar process, which uses the oxide layer as both a protective coating and a mask for doping, so that many transistors can be fabricated and interconnected on a single flat wafer. Fairchild had been founded in 1957 by the "traitorous eight," who left Shockley's laboratory in what became Silicon Valley, a region that took its name from the material at the center of its industry. Robert Noyce, one of the eight, used Hoerni's process to build the first practical monolithic silicon integrated circuit. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments had demonstrated a working integrated circuit months earlier, but his was built on germanium and required wires to connect its parts. Noyce's design could be manufactured at scale, and it was the planar silicon route that grew into the chip industry.

Gordon Moore observed in 1965 that the number of components on a chip was doubling at a regular pace. It began as a projection, but the industry came to treat it as a target and organized its planning around it. For decades, the trend held: chips that once held a few dozen transistors now hold tens of billions, with features measured in nanometers. The raw material is ultra-pure silicon, typically 99.9999999 percent pure or better ("nine nines"), grown as single-crystal ingots and sliced into wafers.

The supply chain behind this is as remarkable as the physics. Advanced fabrication is concentrated in a few firms and places: TSMC in Taiwan and Samsung in South Korea make the most advanced chips, while ASML in the Netherlands is the sole supplier of the extreme ultraviolet lithography machines among the most complex instruments ever built. Computers, smartphones, medical imaging, automobiles, telecommunications, and artificial intelligence all depend on this chain.

Silicon's dominance of computing should not be overstated. Memory, storage, and optical networks also rely on other materials, such as compound semiconductors and magnetic media. But in the logic chips that do the computing, and in the manufacturing base built around them, silicon has no rival.

## Solar Energy and Other Applications

The same logic, abundance, low cost, and a mature manufacturing base, explains silicon's place in solar energy. When light strikes a silicon p-n junction, it frees electrons and produces current. Crystalline silicon cells account for the large majority of solar panels installed worldwide. Manufacturing improvements and scale have cut module prices by roughly 99 percent since the 1970s, making solar power one of the cheapest sources of new electricity in many regions, according to analyses by the International Energy Agency and IRENA. Solar-grade silicon need not be as pure as electronic-grade, but it is still produced in enormous volumes. Here again silicon did not win on efficiency, since other materials can convert light more efficiently, but on cost and scale.

Silicon's other uses fall into three groups:

- **Structural and metallurgical.** Silicon is alloyed with aluminum for engine parts and added to steel to improve its magnetic properties in transformer cores.
- **Photonic.** Silica fibers carry the light signals of the world's optical communications networks.
- **Power and energy.** Silicon carbide, a compound of silicon and carbon, is used for abrasives and high-temperature ceramics and, increasingly, for power electronics in electric vehicles. Silicon is also being explored as a battery anode material, since it can store far more lithium than graphite.

Silicones are a separate family. They are polymers with a backbone of alternating silicon and oxygen atoms and organic groups attached, first studied by Frederic Kipping in the early twentieth century. They are heat-resistant, water-repellent, and flexible, and appear in sealants, lubricants, medical implants, and cookware. They are often confused with silicon but are chemically distinct.

## Challenges: Testing the Thesis

If silicon won through manufacturability, then its weaknesses should lie where manufacturing meets its limits, and they do.

**Environmental cost.** Chip fabrication is energy-intensive and consumes large amounts of ultra-pure water and chemicals; a single large fab can use millions of gallons of water per day. Smelting and polysilicon production carry a significant carbon footprint, which is awkward when the product is meant for clean energy. The footprint depends heavily on the electricity source, which is why much of the industry's recent effort has gone into cleaner power for polysilicon plants.

**Supply-chain fragility.** The concentration of advanced fabrication in Taiwan, South Korea, and a single lithography supplier in the Netherlands makes the chain vulnerable to earthquakes, conflict, and export controls. The shortages of 2020 to 2022 showed how far a disruption can spread, and governments in the United States, Europe, and Asia have since subsidized domestic fabrication as a matter of national strategy.

**Physical limits.** As transistors approach atomic dimensions, quantum effects such as tunneling cause leakage, and heat becomes harder to remove. Moore's trend has slowed: shrinking no longer yields the cost and performance gains it once did. The industry has responded with new transistor geometries, three-dimensional stacking, and specialized architectures rather than simple scaling. Researchers are also investigating complements and alternatives, including gallium nitride, silicon carbide (a challenger to silicon in power devices as well as a silicon compound), two-dimensional materials, photonics, and quantum devices. In solar energy, tandem cells that layer perovskites over silicon aim to surpass silicon's single-junction efficiency limit.

## Conclusion

The thesis holds up under testing, and so do its implications. Silicon's success was never guaranteed. Had germanium's oxide been as stable, or compound semiconductors as easy to manufacture, the industry might look very different. Silicon prevailed through a combination of chemistry, timing, and the accumulated investment of an industry that kept building on the planar process.

That is also why its future is likely to be one of coexistence rather than replacement. Newer materials will take over specific tasks where silicon is weakest, such as high-power switching, light emission, and extreme speed, but each will have to compete with a manufacturing ecosystem refined over seventy years. This is a path-dependence argument, and it cuts both ways: the same lock-in that protects silicon's position could also delay better options. The question for the coming decades is not whether silicon will be displaced, but whether the industry it built can keep paying the environmental and strategic costs of its success.
